lead: Virtual work is a way to solve equilibrium without writing every support reaction. You imagine a tiny, allowed displacement of the system, keeping time frozen, and add the work done by the active forces. At equilibrium that total is zero for every such imaginary displacement. The method is used for linkages, ladders, folding stands and connected beams, where ordinary force and moment equations would carry several unknown reactions. One coordinate, often an angle θ, describes the whole motion.
prereq: You need equilibrium of rigid bodies, the dot product from Unit 1, and basic differentiation.

blocks.text: A virtual displacement δr is an imaginary, infinitesimal change in position. It must be allowed by the supports, and it is taken with time frozen. A pin allows no movement at the pin. A roller on a floor may move along the floor but not into it. A virtual displacement is not a real motion: no load is changed, no time passes, and no velocity is needed.
δU = F · δr = F δr cos θ
blocks.where: δU is virtual work (J), F is the force vector (N), δr is the virtual displacement (m), F and δr are magnitudes, and θ is the angle between them. Work is positive if the force helps the displacement and negative if it opposes.

blocks.text: Ideal reactions do no work. At a smooth pin the point cannot move. At a roller the reaction is normal to the allowed displacement. In a rigid link or an inextensible cable the constraint forces act in equal and opposite pairs, so their total work cancels. Only active forces—weights, applied loads, spring forces—enter the sum.

The principle of virtual work states: a system in equilibrium has δU = 0 for every virtual displacement allowed by its supports. If δU ≠ 0 for an allowed displacement, the system is not in equilibrium. It tends to move in the direction for which δU is positive—opposite to the assumed displacement when δU < 0.

blocks.where: δU is total virtual work (J); F_xi and F_yi are components of active force i (N); δx_i and δy_i are components of its virtual displacement (m). For one coordinate θ, δx = (dx/dθ) δθ and δy = (dy/dθ) δθ.

items: Choose one coordinate θ that fixes the shape, such as a rod angle.
Write x(θ) and y(θ) for every point where an active force acts.
Differentiate to get δx and δy in terms of δθ.
Add the work of each active force with its sign.
Set the total to zero, divide by δθ, and solve for the unknown.

blocks.text: Support reactions disappear, so a ladder or connected-beam problem may need one equation instead of three. A sign in the answer gives direction: a negative P means P acts opposite to the direction you assumed.

figure.caption: The method in four steps; the highlighted step is where equilibrium enters as δU = 0.

spec.aria: The virtual work method: choose one angle, write the positions of the loads in terms of it, set the total virtual work to zero, and solve for the unknown force.

examples.question: A uniform rod AB of length 2 m and weight 200 N is hinged to a vertical wall at A and held by a horizontal force P applied at B. The rod lies above A and makes 30° with the wall. Take x positive away from the wall and y positive upward. Find P by virtual work, giving both sign and direction.
steps: Let θ=30° be the angle between the rod and the wall, L=2 m, and W=200 N at the midpoint G. Assume P positive in the +x direction, away from the wall.
Coordinates: x_B = L sinθ = 2 sinθ, y_B = L cosθ = 2 cosθ; x_G = 1 sinθ, y_G = 1 cosθ. Only the horizontal motion of B and vertical motion of G enter later.
Differentiate: δx_B = 2 cosθ δθ, δy_G = −sinθ δθ. At θ=30°, cosθ=0.8660 and sinθ=0.5000.
Force P: P = (P, 0). δU_P = P δx_B = P(2 cosθ δθ) = 1.732 P δθ J.
examples.answer: P = −57.7 N on the assumed +x direction, so its magnitude is 57.7 N and it acts toward the wall.
examples.check:
import math
theta = math.radians(30.0)
P = -100.0 * math.tan(theta)
print(round(P, 1))
print(round(abs(P), 1))

traps: Giving work to ideal reactions at a smooth pin or roller. The pin point has δr = 0; the roller reaction is perpendicular to the allowed displacement.
Using a real displacement. A virtual displacement is imaginary, infinitesimal and taken with time frozen; supports and cable lengths stay fixed.
Forgetting the chain rule: δx = (dx/dθ) δθ. Do not write δx = dx or leave out δθ.
Sign slip: δU = F·δr = F δr cosθ. Opposite force and displacement gives negative work. A negative unknown means reverse the assumed arrow.
Including internal forces twice. Tension in an ideal rigid link or cable does no net work; use only external active loads.

quiz.a: An imaginary, infinitesimal displacement allowed by the supports, with time frozen.

quiz.q: Why does a smooth roller reaction do no virtual work?
quiz.a: The reaction is normal to the allowed displacement, so F·δr = F δr cos90° = 0.

quiz.q: State the principle of virtual work for a system in equilibrium.
quiz.a: For every virtual displacement allowed by the supports, the total virtual work of active forces is zero: δU = 0.

quiz.q: For the rod in the worked example, find P if θ=45° with the same length and weight.
quiz.a: P = −100 tan45° = −100 N. Magnitude 100 N, acting toward the wall.

quiz.q: Why can the hinge reaction at A be left out of the virtual work equation in the rod example?
quiz.a: The hinge point A has zero virtual displacement. Its reaction force therefore does no work. This does not mean the reaction is zero.

quiz.q: In the rod example, find the virtual work of the weight for δθ=0.01 rad.
What does it mean if δU is negative for an allowed virtual displacement?
quiz.a: δU < 0 for the chosen δr means the active forces oppose that δr. They tend to move the system in the opposite direction, where δU > 0, so the system is not in equilibrium.

beyond: Not for the exam. Virtual work grows into D'Alembert's principle and Lagrange's equations, where generalized coordinates handle many degrees of freedom. Finite element software uses virtual work to build stiffness equations for structures. Robotics uses virtual work and Jacobians to relate static forces to joint torques. Search next: principle of virtual work, generalized coordinates, Lagrange equations, virtual work method in structural analysis.
